core.p: Glycogen is the storage polymer of glucose in liver and muscle. Glycogenesis (synthesis) is stimulated by insulin: glucose‑6‑phosphate → glucose‑1‑phosphate → UDP‑glucose → glycogen synthase adds α‑1,4 links; branching enzyme adds α‑1,6 branches. Glycogenolysis (breakdown) is stimulated by glucagon (liver) and adrenaline (muscle): glycogen phosphorylase cleaves α‑1,4 links producing glucose‑1‑phosphate; debranching enzyme removes α‑1,6 branches. In liver, glucose‑6‑phosphatase converts glucose‑6‑phosphate to free glucose for export; muscle lacks this enzyme, so its glucose‑6‑phosphate enters glycolysis locally.
bullets: Glycogen synthase active when dephosphorylated (insulin → PP1 activation).
Glycogen phosphorylase active when phosphorylated (glucagon/adrenaline → PKA → phosphorylase kinase).
Liver glucose‑6‑phosphatase enables blood glucose release; muscle cannot release free glucose.
Branching enzyme creates α‑1,6 links every 8–12 residues.

callouts.p: Enzyme that adds UDP‑glucose to the non‑reducing ends of glycogen; active when dephosphorylated.
Explains why muscle glycogen cannot directly raise blood glucose.
Do not confuse glycogenolysis (breakdown of glycogen) with gluconeogenesis (new glucose from non‑carbohydrate precursors).

core.p: When glycogen stores are depleted (prolonged fasting), the liver synthesises new glucose via gluconeogenesis. Main substrates: lactate (Cori cycle), glycerol (from lipolysis), glucogenic amino acids (e.g., alanine). Key regulatory enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase, PEPCK, fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphatase, glucose‑6‑phosphatase. Glucagon (via cAMP/PKA/CREB) up‑regulates PEPCK and FBPase transcription. Insulin suppresses these enzymes and promotes lipogenesis: excess glucose → acetyl‑CoA → fatty acid synthesis (via acetyl‑CoA carboxylase, fatty acid synthase) → triglyceride assembly in hepatocytes and adipocytes.
bullets: Gluconeogenesis consumes 6 ATP per glucose formed.
PEPCK is the rate‑limiting step; transcriptionally regulated by glucagon.
Insulin activates acetyl‑CoA carboxylase (via dephosphorylation) → malonyl‑CoA → fatty acid synthesis.
Malonyl‑CoA inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase‑1, blocking fatty acid oxidation.

callouts.p: Synthesis of glucose from non‑carbohydrate precursors (lactate, glycerol, amino acids).
Glucagon ↑cAMP → PKA → CREB → ↑PEPCK mRNA; insulin ↓PEPCK.

For a 6‑mark question on fasting metabolism, list: glucagon ↑ → glycogenolysis → gluconeogenesis (substrates, key enzymes) → glucose release; insulin ↓ → lipolysis ↑ → glycerol & fatty acids → liver uses glycerol for gluconeogenesis, fatty acids for ketogenesis.

core.p: Although detailed treatment belongs to B3.3e, the spec expects you to link the hormone defects to the glucose control mechanisms you have learned. Type 1: autoimmune β‑cell destruction → no insulin → uncontrolled hyperglycaemia, ketogenesis. Type 2: insulin resistance (down‑regulated receptors, post‑receptor defects) + relative insulin deficiency → hyperglycaemia, often with hyperinsulinaemia early on. Both result in failure of the negative‑feedback loop. Treatment aims to restore feedback: insulin injections (type 1), metformin (improves insulin sensitivity), GLP‑1 agonists (enhance glucose‑dependent insulin secretion).
bullets: Type 1 = absolute insulin deficiency; requires exogenous insulin.
Type 2 = insulin resistance + β‑cell exhaustion; lifestyle + oral agents first.
Both cause chronic hyperglycaemia → complications (nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy).
HbA1c reflects average glucose over 2–3 months; used for monitoring.

callouts.p: Reduced cellular response to a given insulin concentration; often due to receptor down‑regulation or signalling defects.
Glycated haemoglobin; diagnostic threshold ≥48 mmol mol⁻¹ (6.5 %).
Do not say type 2 diabetes is caused by ‘too much sugar’; it is multifactorial (genetics, obesity, inactivity).

core.p: Use this table for last‑minute revision. It condenses every spec‑required comparison and the key molecular steps. Memorise the hormone, cell of origin, receptor type, second messenger, main target, and overall effect on blood glucose.
bullets: Insulin: β‑cell, RTK, PIP₃/Akt, liver/muscle/fat, ↓glucose.
Glucagon: α‑cell, GPCR (G_s), cAMP/PKA, liver, ↑glucose.
Negative feedback: glucose ↑ → insulin ↑ → glucose ↓; glucose ↓ → glucagon ↑ → glucose ↑.
Liver is the only organ that can both store and release glucose into blood.
Muscle lacks glucose‑6‑phosphatase → cannot release free glucose.

callouts.p: A receptor that phosphorylates tyrosine residues on itself and downstream proteins upon ligand binding.
The definitive insulin‑dependent glucose uptake step in muscle and fat; exam favourite.
When asked to ‘compare insulin and glucagon’, use a table like this. Examiners award marks for each correct row.

analogy.p: Imagine a house kept at 20 °C. The thermostat (pancreas) senses temperature (blood glucose). When it gets too hot (high glucose), the cooling system (insulin) turns on, removing heat (glucose) by storing it in the walls (glycogen/fat). When it gets too cold (low glucose), the heating system (glucagon) turns on, releasing stored heat from the walls back into the room. Both systems are wired to the same thermostat, so they never run together – the house stays at the set point. Where the analogy breaks down: in the body both hormones are present at low basal levels simultaneously, and the ‘cooling’ and ‘heating’ act on the same organ (liver) rather than separate devices. Also, the body’s set point can shift (e.g., during stress), whereas a simple thermostat has a fixed setting.

terms.d: The maintenance of a constant internal environment despite external changes.
A control mechanism where a change in a variable triggers a response that opposes the change, restoring the set point.
Clusters of endocrine cells in the pancreas that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.
Pancreatic endocrine cell that synthesises and secretes insulin in response to high blood glucose.
Pancreatic endocrine cell that synthesises and secretes glucagon in response to low blood glucose.
A 51‑amino‑acid peptide hormone that lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake, storage and inhibiting hepatic glucose output.
A 29‑amino‑acid peptide hormone that raises blood glucose by stimulating hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
A cell‑surface receptor that autophosphorylates tyrosine residues on ligand binding, initiating a phosphorylation cascade.
A seven‑transmembrane receptor that activates intracellular G‑proteins on ligand binding.
Cyclic adenosine monophosphate; a second messenger that activates protein kinase A.
Phosphatidylinositol‑3‑kinase; generates PIP₃ to recruit Akt to the membrane.
A serine/threonine kinase activated by PIP₃; central mediator of insulin’s metabolic actions.
Insulin‑regulated glucose transporter found in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.
Enzyme that adds glucose units to glycogen; active when dephosphorylated (insulin signalling).
Enzyme that removes glucose‑1‑phosphate from glycogen; active when phosphorylated (glucagon/adrenaline signalling).
Synthesis of glucose from non‑carbohydrate precursors (lactate, glycerol, amino acids) mainly in the liver.
Glycated haemoglobin; reflects average blood glucose over the preceding 2–3 months.

mistakes.w: Insulin is released by α‑cells
mistakes.r: Insulin is released by β‑cells; α‑cells release glucagon.

mistakes.w: Glucagon stimulates glucose uptake in muscle
mistakes.r: Muscle lacks glucagon receptors; glucagon acts only on the liver (and kidney).

mistakes.w: Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis are the same process
mistakes.r: Glycogenolysis = breakdown of glycogen; gluconeogenesis = new glucose from non‑carbohydrate precursors.

mistakes.w: Insulin causes GLUT4 translocation in the liver
mistakes.r: Liver uses GLUT2 (insulin‑independent); GLUT4 is in muscle and adipose.

mistakes.w: cAMP is the second messenger for insulin
mistakes.r: Insulin uses PIP₃/Akt; glucagon uses cAMP/PKA.

mistakes.w: The pancreas detects glucose via GLUT4
mistakes.r: Pancreatic β‑cells use GLUT2 (high‑capacity, low‑affinity) and glucokinase.

mistakes.w: Negative feedback means the hormone stops being secreted completely
mistakes.r: Negative feedback reduces secretion rate; basal secretion continues.

mistakes.w: Type 2 diabetes is caused by eating too much sugar
mistakes.r: Type 2 is multifactorial: genetics, obesity, inactivity leading to insulin resistance and β‑cell dysfunction.

mistakes.w: Glucagon inhibits glycogen synthase directly
mistakes.r: Glucagon activates PKA → phosphorylase kinase → phosphorylates glycogen synthase (inactivates it) and activates glycogen phosphorylase.

mistakes.w: Insulin and glucagon are never present together
mistakes.r: Both hormones circulate at basal levels simultaneously; their relative concentrations determine net effect.

exam.q: State the cell type in the pancreas that secretes insulin and the stimulus for its release.
model: β‑cell (beta cell) of the islets of Langerhans.
Release is stimulated by a rise in blood glucose concentration.
exam.tip: Name the cell and the stimulus; each gets 1 mark.

exam.q: Describe the sequence of events that leads to insulin secretion from a β‑cell when blood glucose rises.
model: Glucose enters β‑cell via GLUT2.
Glucose is phosphorylated by glucokinase, increasing ATP/ADP ratio.
High ATP closes K_ATP channels, causing membrane depolarisation.
Voltage‑gated Ca²⁺ channels open, Ca²⁺ influx triggers exocytosis of insulin granules.
exam.tip: Include GLUT2, glucokinase, ATP, K_ATP channel, Ca²⁺, exocytosis – each step can earn a mark.

exam.q: Explain how insulin lowers blood glucose concentration. Refer to its effects on liver, muscle and adipose tissue.
model: Insulin binds to its receptor tyrosine kinase on target cells.
In liver: activates glycogen synthase → glycogenesis; inhibits glycogen phosphorylase → inhibits glycogenolysis; inhibits gluconeogenic enzymes; promotes lipogenesis.
In skeletal muscle and adipose: triggers translocation of GLUT4 vesicles to the plasma membrane → increased glucose uptake.
In adipose: also inhibits hormone‑sensitive lipase → reduces fatty acid release.
Overall effect: increased glucose removal from blood and storage, lowering blood glucose concentration.
exam.tip: Structure answer by tissue; mention receptor, signalling (Akt), GLUT4, glycogen synthase, and enzyme inhibition.

exam.q: Compare the mechanisms of action of insulin and glucagon. Include receptor type, second messenger and main metabolic effect.
model: Insulin: receptor tyrosine kinase → PIP₃/Akt pathway → promotes glucose uptake (GLUT4) and storage (glycogenesis, lipogenesis).
Glucagon: GPCR (G_s) → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA → activates glycogen phosphorylase and gluconeogenic enzymes → glucose release.
Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises blood glucose.
Insulin acts on liver, muscle, adipose; glucagon acts mainly on liver.
exam.tip: Use a mini‑table in your answer; each correct comparison earns a mark.

exam.q: Describe the role of the liver in the negative‑feedback control of blood glucose.
model: Liver expresses both insulin and glucagon receptors.
When insulin is high: liver takes up glucose, stores as glycogen (glycogenesis) and converts excess to fat (lipogenesis).
When glucagon is high: liver breaks down glycogen (glycogenolysis) and makes new glucose (gluconeogenesis), releasing it into the blood.
These opposing actions return blood glucose toward the set point.
exam.tip: Mention both hormones, both storage and release, and the concept of set point.

exam.q: Explain why muscle glycogen cannot directly contribute to blood glucose homeostasis.
model: Muscle lacks the enzyme glucose‑6‑phosphatase.
Therefore glucose‑6‑phosphate from glycogenolysis cannot be dephosphorylated to free glucose for export.
exam.tip: Name the missing enzyme; that alone often gets both marks.

exam.q: A student claims that ‘cAMP is the second messenger for both insulin and glucagon’. Evaluate this statement.
model: The statement is incorrect.
Insulin uses a receptor tyrosine kinase pathway generating PIP₃ and activating Akt; it does not use cAMP.
Glucagon uses a GPCR → G_s → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA pathway.
exam.tip: State clearly which hormone uses which second messenger.

exam.q: Outline the signalling cascade activated by glucagon in a hepatocyte, from receptor binding to glycogen breakdown.
model: Glucagon binds to its GPCR on the hepatocyte membrane.
Activates G_s protein → stimulates adenylyl cyclase → converts ATP to cAMP.
cAMP activates protein kinase A (PKA).
PKA phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase, which phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase, activating it to catalyse glycogenolysis.
exam.tip: Include GPCR, G_s, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, PKA, phosphorylase kinase, glycogen phosphorylase.

exam.q: During prolonged fasting, blood glucose is maintained. Describe the hormonal and metabolic changes that occur in the liver.
model: Blood glucose falls → α‑cells secrete glucagon; β‑cell insulin secretion falls.
Glucagon binds hepatic receptors → cAMP/PKA cascade.
PKA activates glycogen phosphorylase → glycogenolysis (early fasting).
PKA (via CREB) increases transcription of PEPCK and fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphatase → gluconeogenesis (later fasting).
Substrates: lactate (Cori cycle), glycerol (from adipose lipolysis), amino acids (muscle proteolysis).
Glucose‑6‑phosphatase releases free glucose into bloodstream, maintaining blood glucose.
exam.tip: Separate early (glycogenolysis) and late (gluconeogenesis) phases; name key enzymes and substrates.

exam.q: Explain how insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes leads to hyperglycaemia, referring to the normal insulin signalling pathway.
model: In insulin resistance, insulin binds its receptor but downstream signalling (IRS → PI3K → Akt) is impaired.
Reduced Akt activity means less GLUT4 translocation in muscle and fat → decreased glucose uptake.
In liver, impaired Akt fails to inhibit gluconeogenic enzymes and glycogenolysis → continued hepatic glucose output.
Combined effect: reduced glucose clearance and increased glucose production → chronic hyperglycaemia.
exam.tip: Link each defect (GLUT4, hepatic enzymes) to the normal pathway steps.

worked.q: A 6‑mark question: ‘Explain how insulin lowers blood glucose concentration.’ Provide a model answer structured for full marks.
steps: 1. State that insulin is secreted by pancreatic β‑cells in response to high blood glucose.
2. Describe insulin binding to its receptor tyrosine kinase on target cells (liver, muscle, adipose).
3. Outline the intracellular cascade: receptor autophosphorylation → IRS → PI3K → PIP₃ → Akt activation.
4. For liver: Akt activates glycogen synthase (glycogenesis), inhibits glycogen phosphorylase (inhibits glycogenolysis), inhibits gluconeogenic enzymes (PEPCK, FBPase), stimulates lipogenesis.
5. For muscle and adipose: Akt phosphorylates AS160 → GLUT4 vesicles fuse with plasma membrane → increased glucose uptake.
6. Conclude that these actions increase glucose removal from blood and storage, lowering blood glucose concentration.
worked.ans: Insulin is released from β‑cells when blood glucose rises. It binds to its receptor tyrosine kinase on hepatocytes, myocytes and adipocytes, triggering the IRS‑PI3K‑Akt signalling cascade. In the liver, Akt promotes glycogenesis and lipogenesis while inhibiting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. In muscle and adipose, Akt causes GLUT4 translocation, increasing glucose uptake. The net effect is enhanced glucose removal from the bloodstream and storage, lowering blood glucose concentration.

worked.q: A 4‑mark question: ‘Compare the second messenger systems used by insulin and glucagon.’ Provide a concise answer.
steps: 1. Identify insulin’s receptor as a receptor tyrosine kinase.
2. State that insulin signalling generates the lipid second messenger PIP₃, leading to Akt activation.
3. Identify glucagon’s receptor as a GPCR coupled to G_s.
4. State that glucagon signalling produces the nucleotide second messenger cAMP, activating PKA.
5. Summarise: insulin → PIP₃/Akt; glucagon → cAMP/PKA.
worked.ans: Insulin binds a receptor tyrosine kinase, activating PI3K which produces the membrane lipid second messenger PIP₃, recruiting and activating Akt. Glucagon binds a GPCR linked to G_s, stimulating adenylyl cyclase to generate the nucleotide second messenger cAMP, which activates protein kinase A. Thus insulin uses a PIP₃/Akt pathway, whereas glucagon uses a cAMP/PKA pathway.

bio_ocra.8.6.summary: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) is released from the posterior pituitary when plasma osmolality rises. It acts on the kidneys to increase water re‑absorption, concentrating the urine and restoring normal water balance. This forms a classic negative feedback loop: the stimulus (high osmolality) triggers ADH release, the response (water re‑absorption) reduces the stimulus, and ADH secretion falls again. Understanding this loop is essential for explaining how the body maintains homeostasis of water and solutes.

core.p: ADH, also called vasopressin, is a peptide hormone produced by the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary.
bullets: Synthesised in supra‑optic nuclei of the hypothalamus
Stored in neurosecretory vesicles in the posterior pituitary
Released into the bloodstream in response to increased plasma osmolality or low blood volume

callouts.p: A hormone that increases the permeability of the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct to water, thereby reducing urine volume.

core.h: Stimulus for ADH release – plasma osmolality
core.p: The primary sensor for ADH release is the osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus.
bullets: Osmoreceptors detect changes in plasma osmolality (mOsm kg⁻¹).
When osmolality rises above ~295 mOsm kg⁻¹, they fire more rapidly.
If osmolality falls below ~285 mOsm kg⁻¹, firing rate decreases and ADH release stops.

callouts.p: Normal plasma osmolality ≈ 285‑295 mOsm kg⁻¹.

core.h: Pathway of ADH from brain to kidney
core.p: After synthesis, ADH travels down the hypothalamo‑hypophyseal tract to be released into the systemic circulation.
bullets: Hypothalamic neurones → axons → posterior pituitary → bloodstream
Travels to Vasa recta of the renal medulla

core.p: ADH binds to V2 receptors on the basolateral membrane of principal cells in the collecting ducts.
bullets: Activates adenylate cyclase → ↑cAMP → protein kinase A
PKA phosphorylates aquaporin‑2 (AQP2) vesicles
AQP2 vesicles fuse with the apical membrane, inserting water channels
Water moves from tubular fluid into interstitium (osmosis)
Result: urine becomes more concentrated, volume falls

callouts.p: A water‑channel protein inserted into the apical membrane of collecting‑duct cells in response to ADH.

core.h: Negative feedback loop – step by step
core.p: The whole system works as a classic negative feedback mechanism.
bullets: 1️⃣ Stimulus: plasma osmolality rises (e.g., after drinking salty food).
2️⃣ Sensor: hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect the rise.
3️⃣ Control centre: hypothalamus signals posterior pituitary.
4️⃣ Effector: ADH released → kidneys re‑absorb water.
5️⃣ Response: plasma osmolality falls back toward normal.
6️⃣ Feedback: reduced osmolality decreases osmoreceptor firing → ADH secretion stops.

callouts.p: Negative feedback always acts to *reduce* the original stimulus.

core.h: Effect of ADH on urine volume and concentration
core.p: ADH determines the final urine output and its osmolality.
bullets: High ADH → collecting ducts become permeable → water re‑absorbed → **low urine volume, high urine osmolality**.
Low/absent ADH (e.g., diabetes insipidus) → ducts remain impermeable → **high urine volume, low urine osmolality**.

core.h: Higher‑tier extension – ADH and blood pressure
core.p: ADH also has a vasoconstrictive effect via V1 receptors on blood‑vessel smooth muscle.
bullets: V1‑receptor activation → ↑Ca²⁺ → vasoconstriction
Raises systemic vascular resistance → **increases blood pressure**
Important when both plasma osmolality and blood volume are low

callouts.p: Do not confuse the V1‑mediated vasoconstriction with the water‑re‑absorption effect (V2).

core.p: A disorder of ADH production or response, illustrating the importance of the feedback loop.
bullets: Central DI: insufficient ADH synthesis (hypothalamic damage).
Nephrogenic DI: kidneys fail to respond to ADH (AQP2 defect).
Symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, risk of dehydration.
Treatment: Desmopressin (synthetic ADH) for central DI; thiazide diuretics & low‑salt diet for nephrogenic DI.

callouts.p: Desmopressin mimics ADH and acts on V2 receptors.

core.p: A practical used to assess ADH function.
bullets: Subject abstains from water for several hours.
Measure body weight, plasma osmolality and urine osmolality at intervals.
In a normal response, urine osmolality rises as ADH is secreted.
In DI, urine remains dilute despite rising plasma osmolality.

callouts.p: Remember to note the *direction* of change for each variable – this is what examiners look for.

core.h: Key summary of the ADH feedback loop
core.p: Putting the pieces together:
bullets: **Stimulus** – ↑ plasma osmolality or ↓ blood volume.
**Sensor** – hypothalamic osmoreceptors (and baroreceptors).
**Control centre** – hypothalamus → posterior pituitary.
**Effector** – ADH acts on V2 receptors in kidney (water re‑absorption) and V1 receptors in blood vessels (vasoconstriction).
**Response** – urine volume falls, plasma osmolality returns to normal, blood pressure may rise.
**Feedback** – when normality is restored, ADH secretion stops.

analogy.p: Think of ADH as a thermostat for the body's water level. When the 'room' (blood) gets too dry (high osmolality), the thermostat (hypothalamus) turns the heater (ADH) on, causing the radiator (kidney) to pull in moisture and warm the room back to a comfortable level. The analogy breaks down because a thermostat simply switches on/off, whereas ADH secretion is graded and also affects blood vessels, not just water re‑absorption.

terms.d: A hormone released from the posterior pituitary that increases water re‑absorption in the kidneys by inserting aquaporin‑2 channels into the collecting‑duct cells.
Specialised neurones in the hypothalamus that detect changes in plasma osmolality and alter firing rate accordingly.
The concentration of solutes in blood plasma, expressed in milliosmoles per kilogram (mOsm kg⁻¹).
A water‑channel protein inserted into the apical membrane of collecting‑duct cells in response to ADH.
A G‑protein‑coupled receptor on the basolateral membrane of principal cells in the collecting duct that mediates ADH's water‑re‑absorption effect.
A control mechanism in which the output of a system reduces the original stimulus, restoring the variable to its set point.
The final segment of the nephron where ADH regulates water permeability.
Receptor on vascular smooth muscle that mediates ADH‑induced vasoconstriction.
A disorder characterised by insufficient ADH activity, leading to excessive urine output and thirst.
A synthetic analogue of ADH used to treat central diabetes insipidus.
Pressure‑sensitive receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch that detect changes in blood pressure and can influence ADH release.
Cyclic adenosine monophosphate, a second messenger that rises in collecting‑duct cells after ADH binds to V2 receptors.

mistakes.w: ADH makes the kidneys produce more urine
mistakes.r: ADH **reduces** urine volume by increasing water re‑absorption.

mistakes.w: Osmoreceptors are in the kidney
mistakes.r: Osmoreceptors are located in the hypothalamus, not the kidney.

mistakes.w: ADH acts on the proximal tubule
mistakes.r: ADH acts mainly on the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct.

mistakes.w: Negative feedback means the response continues to increase
mistakes.r: Negative feedback means the response **decreases** the original stimulus.

mistakes.w: High ADH causes high blood pressure only by increasing blood volume
mistakes.r: High ADH also causes vasoconstriction via V1 receptors, contributing to blood pressure rise.

mistakes.w: Diabetes insipidus is caused by high blood sugar
mistakes.r: Diabetes insipidus is a problem with ADH, not glucose; high blood sugar causes diabetes mellitus.

mistakes.w: ADH is a steroid hormone
mistakes.r: ADH is a peptide hormone, not a steroid.

exam.q: Explain how ADH helps to maintain water balance when plasma osmolality rises. (4 marks)
model: Stimulus – plasma osmolality rises above normal.
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the rise and increase firing.
Hypothalamus signals the posterior pituitary to release ADH into the blood.
ADH acts on V2 receptors in the collecting ducts, causing insertion of AQP2 channels, increasing water re‑absorption, reducing urine volume and returning plasma osmolality to normal.
exam.tip: Give the sequence and link each step with the correct term (osmoreceptor, V2 receptor, AQP2).

exam.q: Describe the negative feedback loop that controls water balance. (6 marks)
model: Stimulus – increase in plasma osmolality or decrease in blood volume.
Sensor – hypothalamic osmoreceptors (and baroreceptors).
Control centre – hypothalamus processes the information and signals posterior pituitary.
Effector – ADH released; acts on kidneys (V2) and blood vessels (V1).
Response – water re‑absorption reduces plasma osmolality and raises blood pressure.
Feedback – when normal values are reached, osmoreceptor firing falls and ADH secretion stops.
exam.tip: State each component (stimulus, sensor, control centre, effector, response, feedback) and the direction of change.

exam.q: A patient with diabetes insipidus is unable to concentrate urine. State two possible causes and one treatment for each. (4 marks)
model: Central DI – insufficient ADH production (hypothalamic/pituitary damage). Treatment: Desmopressin (synthetic ADH).
Nephrogenic DI – kidneys do not respond to ADH (AQP2 defect). Treatment: Thiazide diuretic and low‑salt diet.
exam.tip: Use the correct terminology ‘central’ and ‘nephrogenic’; give one treatment per type.

exam.q: Predict what will happen to urine volume and urine osmolality if ADH secretion is blocked. (2 marks)
model: Urine volume will increase (polyuria).
Urine osmolality will decrease (dilute urine).
exam.tip: Link the block to loss of water re‑absorption.

exam.q: Explain why ADH also raises blood pressure. (2 marks)
model: ADH binds to V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle causing vasoconstriction, which increases peripheral resistance and therefore blood pressure.
exam.tip: Mention V1 receptors and vasoconstriction.

exam.q: During a water‑deprivation test, a subject’s plasma osmolality rises from 285 to 300 mOsm kg⁻¹ and urine osmolality rises from 150 to 600 mOsm kg⁻¹. Explain these changes. (4 marks)
model: Water deprivation raises plasma osmolality, stimulating osmoreceptors.
Hypothalamus releases ADH.
ADH increases water re‑absorption in the collecting ducts, concentrating the urine.
Result: plasma osmolality is reduced towards normal and urine becomes more concentrated.
exam.tip: Show cause‑effect for both plasma and urine changes.

exam.q: State the normal range for plasma osmolality and explain what would happen if it fell below this range. (2 marks)
model: Normal range: 285‑295 mOsm kg⁻¹.
If it falls, osmoreceptor firing decreases, ADH secretion stops, kidneys produce a large volume of dilute urine.
exam.tip: Combine normal range with the feedback response.

exam.q: Compare the actions of ADH on the kidney and on blood vessels. (4 marks)
model: Kidney – ADH binds V2 receptors → ↑cAMP → insertion of AQP2 → ↑ water re‑absorption → concentrated urine.
Blood vessels – ADH binds V1 receptors → ↑Ca²⁺ → vasoconstriction → ↑ peripheral resistance → raised blood pressure.
exam.tip: Use receptor types (V2 vs V1) and the downstream effect.

exam.q: Why is ADH release considered a ‘graded’ response rather than an ‘all‑or‑none’ response? (2 marks)
model: The amount of ADH released varies with the degree of change in plasma osmolality; small rises cause small releases, large rises cause larger releases.
exam.tip: Emphasise the proportional relationship.

worked.q: A person drinks 0.5 L of seawater (≈1000 mOsm L⁻¹). Explain how ADH will respond to prevent dehydration.
steps: Calculate extra solute: 0.5 L × 1000 mOsm L⁻¹ = 500 mOsm added to plasma.
Plasma osmolality rises → osmoreceptors fire faster.
Hypothalamus releases ADH.
ADH increases water re‑absorption in the collecting ducts, concentrating urine and conserving water.
Result: plasma osmolality is brought back towards normal, preventing further water loss.
worked.ans: ADH secretion increases, leading to reduced urine volume and higher urine concentration, which helps retain water and restore normal osmolality.

worked.q: In an experiment a rabbit’s plasma osmolality rises from 290 to 310 mOsm kg⁻¹. After 30 min its urine osmolality is 800 mOsm kg⁻¹. Explain the physiological changes that have occurred.
steps: Rise in plasma osmolality activates hypothalamic osmoreceptors.
Posterior pituitary releases ADH into the bloodstream.
ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting‑duct cells, causing AQP2 insertion.
Water is re‑absorbed from the tubular fluid, concentrating the urine to 800 mOsm kg⁻¹.
Re‑absorption reduces plasma osmolality back towards normal.
worked.ans: The rabbit’s kidneys have increased water re‑absorption under ADH control, producing a highly concentrated urine and helping to lower the elevated plasma osmolality.
